q: What is OpenStack and which core services make up a typical private cloud?
a: OpenStack is an open-source cloud operating system that turns a pool of servers, storage and network gear into a self-service infrastructure-as-a-service platform. You consume it through APIs, a CLI and the Horizon dashboard. The core services I always name are Keystone for identity, Nova for compute, Neutron for networking, Glance for images, Cinder for block storage, Placement for resource inventory, and Horizon for the UI. Swift gives object storage, Heat does orchestration, Octavia handles load balancing, and Ironic manages bare metal. Each service exposes a REST API, keeps state in a shared database, and talks to its own agents over a message queue, usually RabbitMQ. In an interview I stress that OpenStack is a set of loosely coupled projects, so you pick the ones you need. A small cloud might run only Keystone, Nova, Neutron, Glance and Cinder.
f: Which services are optional?
How do services authenticate to each other?
p: OpenStack is a set of loosely coupled services exposing REST APIs. The essentials are Keystone (identity), Nova (compute), Neutron (network), Glance (images), Cinder (block storage) and Placement (inventory), with Horizon as the UI.
tip: Say that services share a database and a message bus, then name the minimum viable set.

q: Describe the OpenStack control-plane architecture: API, database, message queue and agents.
a: Every OpenStack service follows a similar shape. An API process receives REST calls and validates the token with Keystone. It writes the desired state to a MariaDB or MySQL database, usually a Galera cluster. For long-running work it casts or calls a message over RabbitMQ using oslo.messaging. Worker daemons, such as nova-conductor, nova-scheduler and nova-compute, or neutron agents, pick up those messages and do the real work on hosts. Results flow back through the queue or the database. This is why RabbitMQ and the database are the two shared dependencies you protect most carefully. If the queue backs up, API calls succeed but nothing happens. If the database is slow, everything slows down. Behind a load balancer such as HAProxy, you run several copies of every API and conductor, which gives horizontal scale and high availability on the controller nodes.
f: Why is nova-conductor needed?
What breaks first when RabbitMQ is unhealthy?
p: API services validate tokens, persist state in Galera, and hand work to workers through RabbitMQ (oslo.messaging). The database and the queue are the shared dependencies to protect.
tip: Explain the failure mode: API accepts the request but no worker consumes it.

q: Walk through what happens, step by step, when a user runs openstack server create.
a: The client first gets a token from Keystone, then calls the Nova API with the flavor, image and network. Nova validates the request, checks quota, and writes an instance record in the database in the building state. The nova-scheduler asks the Placement service for candidate resource providers that have enough vCPU, RAM and disk, then applies filters and weights to choose a host. The conductor sends the build request to nova-compute on that host over the message queue. Compute asks Glance for the image, asks Neutron to create and bind a port, and asks Cinder if there is a volume. Libvirt then defines and starts the guest on KVM. Neutron wires the port with OVS or OVN and DHCP delivers the address. When the guest is running, Nova marks the instance ACTIVE. Knowing this order is how you localise a failure fast.
f: Where does the scheduler get its data?
At which step does a no valid host error appear?
p: Keystone token, Nova API and quota, scheduler with Placement, conductor to compute, then Glance image, Neutron port and Cinder volume, and finally libvirt starts the guest.
cmds: openstack server create --flavor m1.small --image ubuntu-22.04 --network private --key-name mykey web1
openstack server show web1 -c status -c fault
tip: Narrate it in order, then say which log you would open at each step.

q: OpenStack versus VMware vSphere versus Kubernetes: how do you position each?
a: They solve different layers. VMware vSphere is a polished, commercially supported virtualisation stack with strong tooling and licensing cost. OpenStack is an open-source infrastructure API layer that gives you multi-tenant compute, network and storage as a service, with no per-socket licence but real operational effort. Kubernetes orchestrates containers and assumes it already has machines and networks underneath. They are often combined: Kubernetes runs on top of OpenStack VMs or bare metal, using Cinder volumes and Octavia load balancers. I choose OpenStack when an organisation wants a private cloud with self-service, tenant isolation, open APIs, and freedom from licence lock-in, and has a team to run it. I pick VMware when operational simplicity and vendor support outweigh cost. I pick plain Kubernetes when the workloads are all containers and there is no need to offer VMs.
f: When would you not run OpenStack?
How does Kubernetes consume OpenStack?
p: vSphere is a supported virtualisation product, OpenStack is an open IaaS API layer, and Kubernetes orchestrates containers on top of either. They are complementary, not exclusive.
tip: Frame it as layers, not rivals, and be honest about the operational cost of running OpenStack.

q: Explain regions, availability zones, host aggregates and cells. How do they differ?
a: These are four different ways to partition a cloud. A region is a complete deployment with its own API endpoints, usually in a separate site, sharing only Keystone if you choose. An availability zone is a user-visible failure domain inside a region, such as a rack or power zone, which users select to spread instances. A host aggregate is an operator-only grouping of compute hosts with metadata, used for things like GPU hosts, SSD hosts or licence-bound hosts, and tied to flavors through scheduler filters. Cells are a Nova scaling mechanism: each cell has its own database and message queue for its computes, and a top-level API database routes to them. So AZs are for tenants, aggregates are for operators, cells are for scale, and regions are for geography.
f: Can a host be in several aggregates?
Why do cells reduce load on RabbitMQ?
p: Region: a whole deployment. AZ: tenant-visible failure domain. Aggregate: operator grouping with metadata. Cell: scaling shard with its own DB and queue.
tip: Use the one-line summary: AZs for tenants, aggregates for operators, cells for scale.

q: What is the Placement service and why was it split out of Nova?
a: Placement is a small service that tracks inventory and usage of resources. A resource provider, such as a compute node, reports inventories of VCPU, MEMORY_MB and DISK_GB. Consumers, such as instances, claim allocations against those providers. Placement also supports traits, which are qualitative tags like HW_CPU_X86_AVX2 or CUSTOM_GPU, and aggregates and nested providers for things like NUMA nodes and GPUs. Nova used to compute free capacity itself in the scheduler and that was slow and racy. Splitting it out gave a generic, fast, queryable inventory service that Nova, Cyborg and Neutron can all use, for example for bandwidth-aware scheduling. The scheduler now asks Placement for allocation candidates first, then applies filters. When capacity looks wrong, I compare the Placement allocations with what Nova thinks is running, because drift between them causes phantom no valid host errors.
f: What are traits used for?
How do you fix stale allocations?
p: Placement stores resource providers, inventories, allocations and traits. Nova asks it for allocation candidates before running its filters, which is faster and less racy than the old in-scheduler accounting.
tip: Mention allocation drift as the thing you actually debug in production.

q: How does the Nova scheduler pick a host? Explain filters and weighers.
a: Scheduling is a two-stage funnel. First, Placement returns allocation candidates that have enough raw resources. Second, the scheduler runs an ordered list of filters, each of which can reject a host. Common ones are AvailabilityZoneFilter, ComputeFilter, ImagePropertiesFilter, ServerGroupAntiAffinityFilter, NUMATopologyFilter and AggregateInstanceExtraSpecsFilter. Hosts that survive are then ranked by weighers, for example RAMWeigher, which by default spreads load onto the host with most free RAM, or a custom weigher that packs instead. The highest weight wins, with some randomness among the top hosts to avoid stampedes. When you see no valid host was found, the useful move is to read the scheduler log, which prints how many hosts each filter removed, and that tells you whether the issue is capacity, a trait, an aggregate or an affinity rule.
f: Spread versus pack: how do you change it?
How do you debug no valid host?
p: Placement narrows candidates by raw capacity, filters reject hosts on policy, and weighers rank the remainder. The scheduler log shows how many hosts each filter removed.
tip: Say you debug no valid host by reading per-filter counts in the scheduler log.

q: What are flavors and how do you design them well?
a: A flavor defines the size of an instance: vCPUs, RAM, root disk, ephemeral disk and swap, plus extra specs that control behaviour. Extra specs can pin CPUs, request hugepages, set NUMA topology, request a trait through the trait prefix, or select an aggregate. Good flavor design keeps a small, predictable catalogue rather than hundreds of custom sizes, because each one fragments capacity. I group them into families, general purpose, compute optimised, memory optimised, and GPU, with consistent ratios of RAM to vCPU. Root disk sizes are small if instances boot from volume. I make dedicated-CPU flavors public only where needed, and I use private flavors for special tenants. Flavors are immutable in practice, so changing one means creating a new flavor and resizing instances, which is why planning them up front matters.
f: How do you pin CPUs through a flavor?
Why prefer boot from volume with small root disks?
p: A flavor sets vCPU, RAM and disk, and extra specs add pinning, hugepages, traits and aggregate selection. Keep a small catalogue grouped by family to avoid capacity fragmentation.
tip: A short, consistent flavor catalogue is a capacity-planning argument, not just a UX one.

q: Explain the lifecycle and common states of a Nova instance.
a: An instance starts in BUILD while the scheduler, compute, image and network work completes. It becomes ACTIVE when running, SHUTOFF when stopped, and PAUSED or SUSPENDED when the guest is frozen in memory or saved to disk. ERROR means a task failed and the fault field tells you why. Transitional states like RESIZE, VERIFY_RESIZE, MIGRATING, REBUILD and SHELVED_OFFLOADED show an operation in flight, and the separate task state field shows exactly which step. SHELVED_OFFLOADED releases the hypervisor resources and keeps only an image, which is a good way to save capacity for idle servers. DELETED is final, with soft delete optional. In practice I always look at three fields together: status, task_state and power_state, because an instance can be ACTIVE in the database while the guest is actually shut off on the host, and that mismatch is a classic troubleshooting clue.
f: What does VERIFY_RESIZE mean?
How do you reset a stuck instance state?
p: BUILD, ACTIVE, SHUTOFF, PAUSED, SUSPENDED, SHELVED_OFFLOADED, ERROR and DELETED. Check status, task_state and power_state together; a mismatch points at a host-side problem.
cmds: openstack server show web1 -c status -c OS-EXT-STS:task_state -c OS-EXT-STS:power_state
tip: Mention power_state versus status mismatch: it signals the database and the hypervisor disagree.

q: How does cloud-init and the metadata service work in OpenStack?
a: When an instance boots, cloud-init inside the image asks for configuration at the well-known link-local address 169.254.169.254. Neutron makes this reachable through a metadata proxy, either in the router or DHCP namespace, or the OVN metadata agent, which forwards the request to the Nova metadata API and adds headers that identify the instance. Nova returns the hostname, SSH public key, user data and network details. Alternatively, a config drive can be attached as a small read-only disk containing the same data, which works even when there is no network or DHCP. User data is where you inject scripts or cloud-config YAML for first-boot setup. If an instance has no SSH key or user data did not run, I check whether it reached the metadata endpoint from inside the guest, then the metadata agent logs, then whether a config drive would be more reliable.
f: When would you prefer a config drive?
What breaks if the metadata agent is down?
p: cloud-init queries 169.254.169.254, which Neutron proxies to the Nova metadata API. A config drive is the no-network alternative. User data is the first-boot hook.
tip: Name both paths: the network metadata service and the config drive.

q: How are projects, quotas and limits managed, and what happens when a quota is hit?
a: Every resource belongs to a project, formerly called a tenant, and each project has quotas per service: instances, cores, RAM, volumes, gigabytes, floating IPs, security groups and so on. When a user asks for a resource, the service checks current usage against the quota and rejects the request with a quota exceeded error if it would be crossed. Operators set defaults and per-project overrides, and Nova and Cinder can use unified limits through Keystone for a consistent model. Quotas protect shared capacity and prevent one noisy tenant from consuming everything, but they are not guarantees of capacity. They do not reserve hardware. So I pair quotas with capacity monitoring, and I audit usage sync, because after failures the recorded usage can drift from reality and I may need to recount it for a project.
f: Does a quota reserve capacity?
How do you fix quota usage drift?
p: Quotas cap per-project consumption and are enforced at request time. They limit but do not reserve capacity, so combine them with real capacity monitoring.
tip: Be explicit that quota is a ceiling, not a reservation.

q: What is the service catalog and how do endpoints work?
a: The service catalog is the list Keystone returns inside a token response, telling clients where every service lives. Each service, such as compute or network, has endpoints for three interfaces: public, internal and admin, and for each region. Clients use the public endpoint, services talking to each other inside the cloud use the internal endpoint, and administrative operations may use the admin endpoint. This split lets you put public APIs behind a TLS-terminating load balancer with a public name while internal traffic stays on a private network. A common outage cause is a wrong endpoint URL, for example pointing to an old controller IP after a migration, which makes only some services fail. I verify with the catalog, confirm each URL responds, and make sure the region name matches between clients and services.
f: Why separate internal and public endpoints?
What breaks when an endpoint URL is stale?
p: Keystone returns a catalog of services with public, internal and admin endpoints per region. Clients pick by interface and region, so a stale URL breaks only the services that use it.
tip: Mention interfaces and region together, since mismatches are the usual bug.

q: How do OpenStack microversions and API versioning work?
a: Most OpenStack APIs keep a stable major version, for example Compute v2.1, and add features through microversions. A client states the microversion it wants with a header such as X-OpenStack-Nova-API-Version, or the CLI flag os-compute-api-version. The server then behaves as defined for that microversion, and each new minor feature bumps the number. If the client asks for a version higher than the server supports, it gets a clear error, and if it omits the header it receives the baseline behaviour, which keeps old scripts working. The discovery document at the API root lists the minimum and maximum supported versions. For automation I pin an explicit microversion so behaviour does not change under me during upgrades, and I test upgrades by running the same scripts at the old and new maximum.
f: Why pin a microversion in scripts?
How do you find the maximum supported version?
p: Stable major versions, with microversions adding behaviour. Clients opt in through a header; omitting it gives baseline behaviour. Pin the version in automation.
tip: Explain that pinning keeps automation stable across upgrades.

q: What is oslo and why do operators care about it?
a: Oslo is the set of shared Python libraries used by every OpenStack project, so each service does not reinvent the basics. The ones operators meet most are oslo.messaging for RPC over RabbitMQ, oslo.db for database access, oslo.config for configuration files, oslo.log for logging, oslo.policy for authorisation rules, and oslo.cache for caching. Because these are shared, behaviour is consistent: the same config option style, the same log format, the same retry semantics. It also means tuning oslo.messaging, for instance heartbeat and timeout settings, affects all services at once, and a bug there is cloud-wide. When I troubleshoot, I often start with oslo.messaging errors, because a message timeout in one service is usually a symptom of a broken queue, a dead consumer, or clock and network problems rather than a bug in that service itself.
f: Which oslo option would you tune for RabbitMQ flaps?
How does oslo.policy relate to RBAC?
p: Oslo is the shared library layer: messaging, db, config, log, policy and cache. Tuning or bugs there affect every service, which is why messaging errors are the first thing to check.
tip: Say you read MessagingTimeout errors as a queue or consumer symptom, not a service bug.

q: How do you read and manage OpenStack configuration and logs effectively?
a: Each service reads an ini-style file such as nova.conf or neutron.conf, plus drop-in directories in newer releases, and some changes only apply after a restart while others support a mutable reload through SIGHUP. In containerised deployments like Kolla, the configuration is rendered by Ansible and mounted into containers, so I change it in the deployment tooling, never by hand on the host, otherwise the next run overwrites it. For logs, every service writes to its own file or to journald, and a request ID, req-uuid, is propagated across services so I can follow one API call from Nova to Neutron to Cinder. I ship logs to a central system, index by request ID and instance UUID, and keep debug off by default, switching it on for one service temporarily. Good logging discipline is half of OpenStack operations.
f: What is a request ID used for?
How do you enable debug temporarily?
p: ini files per service, reloaded by restart or SIGHUP. In containers, change configuration through the deployment tool. Follow one request across services with its req-id.
tip: The request ID across services is the single best debugging tool; mention it.

q: What does the release cycle look like and how do SLURP releases affect upgrades?
a: OpenStack ships a new release roughly every six months, named alphabetically, for example 2024.1 Caracal and 2024.2 Dalmatian. Each release is supported by the community for a limited maintenance window, with extended maintenance after that. Since 2023.1, the project introduced SLURP, Skip Level Upgrade Release Process, where every other release is designated a SLURP release, and you can upgrade directly from one SLURP release to the next, skipping the one between. That halves the number of upgrade events to roughly one per year while still allowing the intermediate non-SLURP releases for those who want newer features. For planning, I pick a SLURP path, test the upgrade in a staging cloud that mirrors production, read the release notes for removed options and deprecations, and schedule it as a rolling upgrade.
f: What is the difference between SLURP and non-SLURP?
How do you test an upgrade safely?
p: Two releases a year; every other one is a SLURP release you can upgrade between directly, so one planned upgrade per year is possible.
tip: Mention you test the exact upgrade path in staging and read the removed-options notes.

q: How do you check the health of a running OpenStack cloud quickly?
a: I check in layers. First the control-plane services: openstack compute service list and network agent list show whether every nova-compute, scheduler, conductor and neutron agent is up. Second, the shared dependencies, which are Galera cluster size and sync state, RabbitMQ cluster status and queue depth, and the HAProxy backends. Third, a real functional probe: create a tiny instance, attach a floating IP, ping it and delete it, which exercises Keystone, Nova, Glance, Neutron and the data plane together. I automate that as a canary every few minutes. Fourth, resource headroom, meaning hypervisor usage, Ceph capacity and placement allocations. Fifth, logs and alerts for errors and stuck instances. A green service list with a failing canary tells you the problem is in the integration or data plane, not in a daemon.
f: What would your canary test include?
Which metric tells you RabbitMQ is struggling?
p: Check service and agent lists, Galera and RabbitMQ state, run a synthetic canary that boots a VM and pings it, then check capacity headroom.
tip: A synthetic end-to-end canary catches what a green service list misses.

q: What is Horizon and when do you prefer the CLI, SDK or API instead?
a: Horizon is the Django web dashboard that lets users and admins manage projects, instances, networks and volumes, and it just calls the public APIs, so anything it does you can also do elsewhere. I use it for quick exploration and for users who are new to the cloud. For daily operations and automation I prefer the unified openstack CLI because it is scriptable and consistent across services, and for programmatic work I use openstacksdk in Python or the Terraform and Ansible providers, which give repeatable, reviewable infrastructure. Raw REST calls are mostly for debugging when I want to see headers and microversions. A key operational point is authentication: clouds.yaml keeps credentials and endpoints for multiple clouds and projects, so the same tooling works everywhere without sourcing environment files by hand.
f: What is clouds.yaml?
Why is infrastructure as code better than Horizon clicks?
p: Horizon is a UI over the same APIs. Use the openstack CLI for scripting, openstacksdk, Terraform or Ansible for repeatable automation, and clouds.yaml for credentials.
tip: Say that anything repeatable belongs in code, not in dashboard clicks.

q: How do images work in Glance and what formats do you use?
a: Glance stores and serves virtual machine images and their metadata. An image has a disk format, such as qcow2, raw, vmdk or iso, and a container format, usually bare. With a Ceph backend, I convert images to raw so that instances can be created as copy-on-write clones of the image in RBD, which makes boot take seconds instead of copying gigabytes. Images have visibility settings, private, shared, community or public, and properties like hw_disk_bus, hw_vif_model and os_distro that tell Nova how to present hardware to the guest. I keep golden images small, patched regularly, with cloud-init installed and no secrets inside, and I sign them where possible. Glance also supports multiple backends and image caching on compute hosts for speed.
f: Why raw images on Ceph?
How do you control who can see an image?
p: Glance stores images with format and metadata properties. On Ceph, use raw so boots are instant copy-on-write clones. Keep golden images small, patched and secret-free.
cmds: openstack image create --disk-format raw --container-format bare --file ubuntu.raw --public ubuntu-22.04
qemu-img convert -f qcow2 -O raw ubuntu.qcow2 ubuntu.raw
tip: The raw-on-Ceph point shows you understand the storage and compute interaction.

q: Explain live migration: how it works, its requirements and common failures.
a: Live migration moves a running instance between compute hosts with minimal downtime. Libvirt copies the guest memory pages iteratively to the destination while the guest keeps running, then briefly pauses it, transfers the last dirty pages and the CPU state, and resumes it on the target. With shared storage such as Ceph, only memory moves. Without shared storage, block migration also copies the disk, which is much slower. Requirements are compatible CPU models between hosts, reachable libvirt and migration ports, consistent networking, matching image and volume access, and enough destination capacity. Common failures include CPU feature mismatches, a guest dirtying memory faster than it can be copied so it never converges, firewalls blocking ports, and mismatched Neutron port binding. Tools to help include auto-converge, post-copy and a configurable downtime limit.
f: How do you handle a guest that never converges?
What CPU mode do you set for migration-friendly clouds?
p: Libvirt pre-copies memory while the guest runs, then pauses briefly to finish and resume on the target. Shared storage keeps it quick; CPU model mismatches and high dirty rates are common failures.
tip: Name auto-converge and post-copy as the answer for busy guests.

q: What is the difference between cold migration, resize, evacuate and rebuild?
a: They look similar but serve different situations. Cold migration shuts the instance down, moves it to another host and starts it again, and is used for maintenance when live migration is not possible. Resize changes the flavor, and because the new size may not fit the old host, it also moves the instance; the state VERIFY_RESIZE lets the user confirm or revert. Evacuate is for failure: when a compute host is dead, you rebuild its instances on another host, keeping the same UUID, network ports and volumes, and for shared-storage setups the disk survives. Rebuild reinstalls an instance from a new or same image on the same host, wiping the root disk. Picking the right one is a classic scenario question, with the key words being planned versus failed host, and keep data versus reinstall.
f: What data is lost on rebuild?
What must be true before you evacuate?
p: Cold migrate: planned move with downtime. Resize: new flavor, may move. Evacuate: recover from a dead host. Rebuild: reinstall the root disk from an image.
tip: Frame it as planned versus failed host, and data kept versus wiped.

q: What is CPU pinning and NUMA awareness, and when do you need them?
a: Modern servers have multiple NUMA nodes, where memory and PCI devices are closer to certain cores. A guest that spans nodes pays a latency penalty for remote memory. With the flavor property hw:cpu_policy set to dedicated, Nova pins each guest vCPU to a specific host physical core, and with hw:numa_nodes it keeps the guest on specified NUMA nodes, aligning memory and vCPUs. Combined with hugepages, this gives predictable low latency and is standard for telco, NFV, databases and high-performance workloads. The trade-off is that pinned instances cannot be overcommitted and reduce scheduling flexibility, so I place them in a dedicated host aggregate, reserve host cores for the OS using cpu_dedicated_set and cpu_shared_set, and use separate flavors. For ordinary web workloads, shared CPUs with overcommit are the better cost choice.
f: Why separate dedicated and shared CPU sets?
What does hw:cpu_thread_policy do?
p: hw:cpu_policy=dedicated pins vCPUs to cores and NUMA settings keep memory local. Great for latency-sensitive loads, but no overcommit, so isolate with aggregates.
cmds: openstack flavor set rt --property hw:cpu_policy=dedicated --property hw:numa_nodes=1
tip: State the trade-off: performance and predictability versus density.

q: How do hugepages help, and how are they configured for instances?
a: Normal memory uses 4 KB pages, so large guests need many page-table entries, and the CPU translation cache, the TLB, misses often. Hugepages, typically 2 MB or 1 GB, cut that overhead and improve memory-intensive and packet-processing workloads, and they are required for DPDK. On the host you reserve hugepages at boot with kernel parameters, so they are not fragmented, and you tell Nova how much memory is for hugepages. On the instance side you set the flavor property hw:mem_page_size to large, 2MB or 1GB. Hugepage memory is not swappable and not shared with normal allocations, so you must size reservations carefully; too many starves normal guests and the host, too few causes scheduling failures. I also remember that guests with hugepages cannot use memory overcommit.
f: Why are hugepages needed for DPDK?
What happens if hugepages are exhausted?
p: Hugepages reduce TLB misses for big or packet-heavy guests. Reserve them at host boot, set hw:mem_page_size on the flavor, and accept no memory overcommit.
tip: Link hugepages to DPDK and NFV to show you know the use case.

q: How do CPU and RAM overcommit ratios work and how do you choose them?
a: Overcommit lets the scheduler allocate more virtual resources than physical ones, because most guests are idle most of the time. The cpu_allocation_ratio and ram_allocation_ratio are set per compute node, or through Placement inventory, with typical defaults of 16 for CPU and 1.5 for RAM. CPU overcommit is relatively safe because the kernel scheduler time-slices, but it hurts latency under contention; I watch steal time and load. RAM overcommit is riskier, because exhausting host memory triggers swapping or the OOM killer, so I use a low ratio like 1.0 to 1.2 for production. Disk can be overcommitted with thin provisioning but needs monitoring. I choose ratios by workload class, conservative for databases and latency-sensitive tenants, higher for dev and test aggregates, and I confirm with real utilisation data, not guesses.
f: Which metric shows CPU contention?
Where do you set the ratio so it is respected by Placement?
p: Allocation ratios let scheduling exceed physical capacity. CPU 4 to 16 is common, RAM close to 1. Set per aggregate by workload and watch steal time and memory pressure.
cmds: openstack resource provider inventory show <uuid> VCPU
tip: Say conservative for databases, aggressive for dev, and validate with steal time.

q: What are Nova cells v2 and why would you deploy them?
a: Cells v2 is Nova's horizontal scaling design. The top level has the API database, which holds instance mappings and host mappings, and the API services. Below that, each cell has its own database and message queue, serving a group of compute nodes. A request is routed to a cell by the scheduler and conductor, and the instance data lives in that cell. This bounds the size of any one RabbitMQ cluster and database, which are the usual bottlenecks at a few thousand compute nodes, and it gives a failure domain, since a broken cell affects only its hosts. There is always at least cell0, which holds instances that failed to schedule, and a default cell1. I would introduce extra cells when node counts, message rates or upgrade blast radius justify the added complexity.
f: What is cell0 for?
Which services run per cell versus globally?
p: Cells split compute nodes into groups with their own DB and queue under a global API database. They bound RabbitMQ and DB load and limit failure blast radius.
tip: Cells are about bounding the message bus and DB, not about regions.

q: A compute node dies. What is your recovery procedure?
a: First confirm it is really down, not just a service issue, by checking the host, the hypervisor in nova and the console or BMC. If it is dead, I fence it so it cannot come back and corrupt shared disks, which is critical with shared storage. I mark the service forced down so Nova stops waiting for it, then evacuate the instances to healthy hosts, either one by one or in bulk with the host-evacuate approach. Instances on shared storage such as Ceph keep their disk and boot again with the same identity. Instances on local ephemeral disk lose data, so I tell the owners. I then check that ports, volumes and floating IPs are re-bound, repair or replace the hardware, and re-enable the service. Afterwards I review why detection and recovery were not automatic and add monitoring or Masakari.
f: Why fence before evacuate?
What is Masakari?
p: Verify the failure, fence the host, force the service down, evacuate instances (shared storage preserves disks), verify networking, then repair and re-enable. Automate with Masakari.
tip: Always say fencing comes before evacuation; that is the data-safety point.

q: How do server groups and affinity rules work?
a: A server group is a policy container that you attach to instances at boot using a scheduler hint. The policies are affinity, which places all members on the same host, anti-affinity, which forces them onto different hosts, and the soft variants that try but do not fail the build. The common use is high availability: put the replicas of a database or a stateless tier into an anti-affinity group so one host failure cannot take them all out. The limitation is that anti-affinity needs enough hosts, so a strict group of five on a three-host cloud will fail with no valid host. Also, the rule is enforced at build and during live migration and evacuate, which can block maintenance. I use soft anti-affinity when capacity is tight, and strict where the application truly cannot survive co-location.
f: What is the difference between anti-affinity and soft anti-affinity?
How does anti-affinity affect maintenance?
p: Server groups with anti-affinity spread replicas across hosts and affinity co-locates them. Strict policies fail when hosts run out, so use the soft variant when capacity is tight.
cmds: openstack server group create --policy anti-affinity db-group
openstack server create --hint group=<group-id> --flavor m1.large --image ubuntu db1
tip: Mention that strict anti-affinity can block live migration during maintenance.

q: How do you provide GPUs to instances: passthrough versus vGPU?
a: There are two main approaches. With PCI passthrough, a whole physical GPU is assigned to one instance through VFIO, giving near native performance but no sharing. You enable IOMMU, whitelist the device in nova.conf, create a flavor with a pci alias, and Nova schedules onto hosts with a free device. With vGPU, an NVIDIA or similar driver splits one card into mdev types, and Nova assigns those virtual devices to several instances, which raises utilisation and suits VDI and smaller inference jobs, though it needs vendor licences and has migration limits. I choose passthrough for heavy training and full-card workloads, and vGPU for shared, smaller workloads. Either way I put GPU hosts in a dedicated aggregate, tag them with traits so the scheduler is precise, and monitor temperature, memory and utilisation with the vendor exporter.
f: What is needed on the host for passthrough?
What are the migration limits of vGPU?
p: Passthrough gives a whole GPU to one guest with full performance. vGPU shares a card across guests. Use aggregates and traits to schedule precisely.
tip: State the trade-off: dedicated performance versus utilisation.

q: An instance is stuck in a transitional state such as BUILD or deleting. How do you fix it?
a: First I find out why, not just reset it. I look at the instance fault and task_state, then the nova-compute log on the host, using the request ID, to see what step hung: maybe image download, a Neutron port that never became active, a Cinder attach, or a libvirt error. If the underlying operation is gone, for example the compute service restarted mid-task, the database still shows the old task state, and the safe cleanup is to reset the state with openstack server set --state error, then delete or rebuild it. For a stuck delete I check for leftover ports, volumes and libvirt domains, which often block cleanup. I avoid editing the database directly except as a documented last resort. Afterwards I add a periodic job or alert for instances in the same state over a time threshold.
f: What is the safe way to reset an instance?
How do you detect stuck instances proactively?
p: Read fault, task_state and the compute log by request ID to learn what hung. Then reset state to error and delete or rebuild; clean up ports and volumes. Alert on long-lived transitional states.
cmds: openstack server show web1 -c fault -c OS-EXT-STS:task_state
tip: Diagnose before resetting; resetting hides the cause.

q: What hypervisors does Nova support and why is KVM the default choice?
a: Nova supports several drivers through a compute driver interface. KVM through libvirt is by far the most used, and it is the best-tested path with all features such as live migration, NUMA, hugepages, vGPU and SR-IOV. Others include QEMU in pure emulation for testing, VMware vCenter, where Nova talks to vSphere, Hyper-V, and Ironic for bare metal instead of virtual machines. LXC and Virtuozzo drivers exist but see far less use. I choose KVM because it is open source, integrated in the Linux kernel, supported by every major distribution, performs close to bare metal with hardware virtualisation, and has the strongest community and vendor support. The decision to use VMware as a Nova backend usually comes from an existing investment, but then you lose several OpenStack-native features.
f: When would you use the VMware driver?
What does Ironic add?
p: KVM via libvirt is the mainstream, best-tested driver. Others exist, such as VMware, Hyper-V and Ironic for bare metal, but KVM has the richest feature support.
tip: Answer with KVM and give one reason beyond cost, such as feature coverage.

q: How do you perform maintenance on a compute node without user impact?
a: I plan it as a controlled drain. First I disable the compute service so the scheduler stops placing new instances there, with a reason recorded. Then I live-migrate instances away, in batches, checking that each migration completes and the guest remains reachable. Instances that cannot be live-migrated, such as those with pinned devices, get coordinated downtime or a cold migration with the owner informed. Once empty, I perform the work, such as a kernel patch, firmware update or hardware fix, then reboot, verify libvirt, nova-compute and the Neutron agent are healthy, and re-enable the service. For large fleets I use host aggregates and automation with Ansible, and I respect anti-affinity groups and capacity so the drain does not overload remaining hosts. Communication and a rollback plan complete the procedure.
f: What can block a drain?
How do you automate the loop for many hosts?
p: Disable the service, live-migrate instances in batches, handle non-migratable guests with coordination, do the work, verify agents, re-enable. Watch capacity and anti-affinity.
cmds: openstack compute service set --disable --disable-reason 'kernel patch' <host> nova-compute
openstack server list --host <host> --all-projects -f value -c ID | xargs -n1 openstack server migrate --live-migration
tip: Say disable first, drain, work, verify, enable, in that order.
